title: Amortization Schedule—Breaking Down the Monthly Payment

cards.front: How do you calculate the monthly interest on a mortgage?
back: $$\text{Monthly Interest} = \text{Loan Balance} \times \frac{\text{APR}}{12}$$
The monthly rate is the annual percentage rate divided by 12.
Interest is computed on the balance at the beginning of the month.

cards.front: How is the principal portion of a mortgage payment determined?
back: $$\text{Principal Payment} = \text{Monthly Payment} - \text{Monthly Interest}$$
The rest of the payment after paying interest reduces the loan balance.
The principal portion grows as the balance shrinks.
A table showing each payment, the split between interest and principal, and the remaining loan balance.
It illustrates how the balance declines to zero over the loan term.
The last payment may be slightly adjusted to bring the balance exactly to $0.

cards.front: Build the first month of an amortization schedule: Loan $200,000, APR 6%, monthly payment $1,199.10.

back: Interest is calculated on the declining loan balance.
As you pay down principal, the balance gets smaller.
A smaller balance means less interest accrues each month.
cards.front: Why does the interest portion decrease over time?

back: Sum the interest column for all payments.
It should equal (Monthly Payment × Number of Payments) – Original Loan Amount.
Slight differences may occur due to rounding of the final payment.
cards.front: How can you verify the total interest from an amortization schedule?
What happens to the principal portion of each payment as the loan matures?
back: The principal portion increases over time.
Because less interest is due each month, more of the fixed payment goes toward principal.
This accelerates the payoff toward the end of the loan.
It directly reduces the loan balance, which decreases future interest.
The loan is paid off faster, and total interest is reduced.
[[imp:Even small extra payments early in the term save significant interest.]]
cards.front: How does an extra principal payment affect the mortgage?

back: Total principal reduction = Scheduled Principal + Extra Payment.
New Balance = Old Balance – Total Principal Reduction.
The extra amount goes entirely to principal.

What should the final balance be in a complete amortization schedule?
back: $0 (or very close; the last payment may be adjusted).
The loan is fully paid off after the last payment.
Any rounding difference is cleared in the final month.

cards.front: What is the blueprint for building an amortization schedule?
